approved: Enhancing Online Safety for Children (Consequential Amendments) Bill 2014
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill is part of a package creating a Children's e-Safety Commissioner and a complaint system to quickly remove harmful cyber-bullying material from major social media sites.

The Commissioner, an independent office within the Australian Communications and Media Authority, would manage the complaint system and could order social media services to take down material targeting a child within 48 hours.
The bill sets up a two-tiered system where social media services can be declared Tier 1 (self-regulating) or Tier 2 (directly regulated, with civil penalties for non-compliance).
Creates the Children's e-Safety Commissioner and specifies powers and functions.
Establishes a complaints system for cyber-bullying material targeting an Australian child.
Sets up a 2-tiered scheme for rapid removal of such material from large social media services.
Allows the Commissioner to issue end-user notices requiring removal, cessation, or apology.
Transfers administration of the online content scheme under the Broadcasting Services Act 1992 from ACMA to the Commissioner.
Australian children, parents and guardians of children, and providers of large social media services are affected.

Introduced the Enhancing Online Safety for Children Bill establishing a Children's e-Safety Commissioner with a two-tiered enforcement system, citing figures that up to 40 per cent of teenagers to age 16 have experienced cyberbullying, and said noncompliant services could be fined up to $17,000 per day.

Supported the online safety legislation as a member of the coalition's Online Safety Working Group, noting more than half of children now have access to or ownership of an internet-connected device before they turn 10, and recounted a Darwin case where schoolchildren set up a hurtful Facebook gossip page targeting a fellow student.

Supported the online safety bill, citing University of New South Wales research that 72 per cent of schools reported at least one cyberbullying incident in 2013, and estimated around 463,000 Australian children aged eight to 17 are cyberbullying victims, of whom about 365,000 are in the peak age group of 10 to 15.

Summed up debate on the Enhancing Online Safety for Children Bill 2014, noting the bill followed more than 80 submissions to a January 2014 discussion paper and 29 submissions to a Senate committee reporting by 3 March, and quoted Twitter's global chief executive Dick Costolo admitting the company has sucked at dealing with abuse and trolls on its platform.
